solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Superhero hit the face of Magneto with one end of weapon

parts.note: to bat is to strike, as with a cricket or baseball bat

indicators.note: the face of something is its front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the front letter of the villain's name
one and 'a' are interchangeable

indicators.note: an end is an extremity, and here the closing extremity of the word is the letter kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A comic-book hero lands a blow on his foe Magneto's face using the tip of a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The superhero and Magneto share a comic-book world, which is the disguise: Magneto only lends his first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Batman is the caped DC Comics crime-fighter, one of the best-known costumed heroes.

clue.text: Colour of something one might wipe with the middle of hanky

parts.note: you mop your forehead when sweating

indicators.note: the middle is the central point, so only the central letter of the five-letter word is kept

parts.note: the third of five letters

explanation.surface: It sounds like a grubby question about what colour a used handkerchief turns.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'something one might wipe' is a cryptic pointer to the forehead; the hanky is only there to supply its centre letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown is a basic hue, the shade of earth, wood and chocolate.

clue.text: Antisocial housebreaker retching violently having injected heroin

indicators.note: an injection puts one thing inside another, so a letter goes in among the rest
something done violently is thrown about, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be scrambled
H is drug slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A burglar with a drug habit is heaving violently after a fix of heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: The heroin letter joins the fodder before it is mixed. 'Antisocial housebreaker' is a playful description: the Dr Seuss character creeps into Whoville homes to steal Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dr Seuss character hates festive cheer and sneaks into houses to steal presents and decorations, so he is a grumpy burglar.

clue.text: Film a crazy woman performing a flip

parts.note: taken as written
mad means crazy

indicators.note: a flip turns something over, so the name is written back to front

parts.note: a woman's name

explanation.surface: A film about an unhinged woman doing somersaults.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman' in crosswords is often any female first name; here a three-letter one is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1984 Milos Forman movie about Mozart won the Best Picture Oscar.

clue.text: By the conclusion of erotica, Bet is excited

indicators.note: by means beside, so one piece sits next to the other
a conclusion is an ending, so the final letter is kept

parts.note: the word ends in this letter
a small wager is a flutter in British slang

explanation.surface: Someone called Bet gets worked up as she finishes reading something racy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bet' looks like a woman's name but is a wager; in Britain a flutter is a small bet, as on a horse race. 'Erotica' gives only its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a flutter means nervously agitated, so the adjective describes someone stirred up and excited.

clue.text: Fellow shocked nun by spinning a certain body part

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for fellow

indicators.note: something shocked is jolted out of place, so the letters are jumbled
spinning things whirl round into new positions, reinforcing the instruction to rearrange

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange
'a certain person' can be 'one', a single unnamed individual

explanation.surface: A man startles a nun by twirling a particular part of his body.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words point to the same jumble of the nun-by letters; 'a certain' then stands for an indefinite someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The funny bone is the spot at the elbow where the ulnar nerve sits, tingling sharply when knocked.

clue.text: Discover blue planet supporting advocates for peace

indicators.note: in a down answer a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes second

parts.note: the United Nations exists to keep the peace
our world is the blue planet

explanation.surface: Peace campaigners are backing efforts to find a new blue world.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue order puts the planet first, but 'supporting' places it below the peacekeepers in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig something up from the ground, literally or figuratively, is to find it out.

clue.text: Giant bird sang after the removal of its wings

indicators.note: after means following, so this piece is placed later in the answer

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird

indicators.note: wings are the side parts, so stripping them leaves only the inner letters

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A huge bird went on singing even after its wings had been taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' sounds avian, fitting the bird, but here it means the outer letters of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were the colossal deities of Greek myth, so the word names any person or thing of enormous size or power.

clue.text: Get back on steamship stopped by some officers

indicators.note: something stopped by an obstacle is interrupted, so another group is pushed into the middle

parts.note: re means on or concerning
a posse is a band of law officers
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: Climbing back aboard a steamer is blocked by a few officials.
explanation.walkthrough: The officers break into the 'on steamship' pair, landing between its two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Repossessing means reclaiming goods, typically when payments lapse, so it is regaining ownership.

clue.text: The twenty-fifth can is very small

parts.note: a tin is a can
the 25th letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: The can numbered twenty-five is a little one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The twenty-fifth' reads as a date or rank, but it is the alphabet's 25th letter, and it comes second.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean minute or minuscule in size, simple synonyms.

clue.text: Running round and exercising beside allotment

indicators.note: beside means next to, so one part follows on from the other

parts.note: the letter is round in shape
physical education, school exercise
a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: Jogging laps and working out next to a plot where vegetables grow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' and 'allotment' both suggest exercise and gardening; an allotment is a British rented vegetable plot, but here it means a portion.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that is running is in operation, so the noun names the state of functioning.

clue.text: Finish crossword setter's tea?

parts.note: straight meaning: to consume a meal completely
a setter loves to mix letters, so in their hands the drink becomes a jumbled version of itself, the word stirred 'up'

explanation.surface: It reads like urging someone to drain the cup of tea a puzzle-maker has brewed.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: a crossword setter rearranges 'tea' into a mixed-up verb, which is exactly what an anagrammatist does with it.
explanation.definitionFit: To clear your plate entirely is the everyday phrasal verb for completing a meal.

clue.text: Where toddlers are sure to be trained in number lines

indicators.note: in means inside, so the jumbled letters go within the others
training something reshapes it, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange
N is the abbreviation for number
RY stands for railway, railway lines

explanation.surface: Small children are bound to be taught to line up in numbered rows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' in crosswords often means railway lines, abbreviated RY; the rearranged word sits between number and lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A nursery is the room or school where very young children are cared for.

clue.text: Why, ultimately, without an R, typeface's pants

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the final letter is kept

parts.note: the word's closing letter

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the other letters wrap around

parts.note: a font is a typeface, plus the possessive s
the letter itself

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a font's lettering looks pants without an R, pants being British slang for rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but in its old sense of outside it wraps the font word around the R. Y-fronts are British men's briefs; pants in Britain means underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are men's briefs with an inverted-Y seam at the front, and British pants are underwear.

clue.text: Extra sweaty smell accompanying group of students

indicators.note: accompanying means going alongside, so one piece is set next to the other

parts.note: BO is body odour
the National Union of Students, the British student body

explanation.surface: An additional whiff of sweat comes along with a crowd of students.
explanation.walkthrough: NUS is Britain's National Union of Students, a familiar crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonus is something additional, given on top of what is expected.

clue.text: Order patients' spines to be examined on these?

definitions.text: spines to be examined on these?

parts.note: to book is to reserve or order
doctors call patients cases

explanation.surface: Instructions for patients' backbones to be checked, as if on a couch.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface pushes spines towards backbones, but the spines are those of books on shelves; 'patients'' supplies a doctor's word for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Book spines face outward on shelving units, so they are what you scan when browsing a library cabinet.

clue.text: Revolutionary put on inordinately silly hat, causing complaint

indicators.note: placed on top of in an across answer means attached after

parts.note: too means excessively

indicators.note: silly means daft or muddled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange
Che Guevara, the Marxist revolutionary

explanation.surface: A rebel donned an absurd hat, and people grumbled.
explanation.walkthrough: The revolutionary is read first but comes last: 'put on' means he is tacked onto the rest. Che is the usual crossword revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: In medical parlance a complaint is an ailment, and a pain in the teeth is one such.

clue.text: Experiment delivered with old German's instruments

indicators.note: a speech is delivered by voice, so the word is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: to try is to experiment
the Angles were a Germanic people who settled in England

explanation.surface: An experiment was carried out using the tools of a German from long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' seems to describe the experiment being handed over, but it means spoken; the Angles were the old Germanic tribe that gave England its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The triangle is a percussion item, a bent steel bar struck with a beater in orchestras.

clue.text: Make prisoner parade about inside

parts.note: a con is a convict

indicators.note: inside means within, so one letter sits in the middle of another word

parts.note: to strut is to parade showily
C is circa, about

explanation.surface: An order to make an inmate march around indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a containment instruction, but it is the letter C for circa, which goes inside the parade word.
explanation.definitionFit: To construct is to build or assemble, a direct synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Oscar? He writes plays in a different way

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: to play with something is to toy with it, so the letters are moved about

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Oscar Wilde, perhaps: he writes plays, unlike most people.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar and plays suggest Wilde the dramatist, but Oscar is just a radio-alphabet letter and 'plays' is a verb telling you to mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means differently or in another manner, as in 'he thinks otherwise'.

clue.text: Rerelease the 2nd part of Pullman's boring novel series

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so one letter goes inside
novel means new, so the letters take a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: the second part of a word is its second letter

parts.note: the second letter of the author's name

explanation.surface: Republish volume two of Philip Pullman's dull fiction sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel series' looks like Pullman's His Dark Materials, but 'novel' is the mixing signal and 'boring' places a letter into the result.
explanation.definitionFit: To reissue is to publish or put out again, which is what rereleasing means.

clue.text: Overcome by pride and greed, perhaps, knight falls

indicators.note: to be overcome by something is to be surrounded and swamped, so one letter is enclosed

parts.note: two of the seven deadly sins
K stands for knight in British honours such as KBE

explanation.surface: A knight brought low by vanity and avarice comes crashing down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that pride and greed are examples of a category, the deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that drops or goes down, like a ship or the sun, is said to sink.

clue.text: Sleet swirls around empty ancient city

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the mixed letters surround the others
swirling things are churned about, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its contents, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Icy rain blows round the deserted ruins of an old town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient city' wants to be the definition; only 'city' is, while 'empty ancient' is the outside of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Seattle is the largest settlement in Washington State, famously rainy, so it is a city.

clue.text: Copper joins mum and I on the edge of snooker table

indicators.note: joining means linking up, so the parts are placed side by side

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
keeping mum means staying quiet, and sh calls for silence
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A policeman joins my mother and me beside the snooker table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'mum' look like a police officer and a mother; they are the chemical symbol and a call for silence.
explanation.definitionFit: On billiard and snooker tables the rubber-lined rails that balls bounce off are named cushions.

clue.text: Plug Shrewsbury's top circus performers

parts.note: to plug a gap is to seal it

indicators.note: the top of a down word is its first letter

parts.note: the town's opening letter

explanation.surface: An advert boosting the best entertainers in Shrewsbury, a market town in Shropshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plug' suggests promoting, but it is a stopper.
explanation.definitionFit: Trained sea mammals balancing balls on their noses were classic big-top acts.

clue.text: Broadcast jazz vocalist singing nonsense?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to spread widely, as seed is sown
second meaning: someone who scats, improvising wordless syllables

explanation.surface: A jazz singer on the radio, crooning meaningless syllables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' tempts as radio, but it is the farmer's sense of throwing seed. The question mark warns the second sense is a made-up word, one who scats.
explanation.definitionFit: To spread seed by hand is to strew it widely; and scat singing uses nonsense syllables, so a scat singer could jokingly be named this.

clue.text: Oddly, Shaggy put on a medieval Icelandic piece

indicators.note: put on means attached, so another piece follows
oddly means taking the odd-numbered positions only

parts.note: first, third and fifth letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Strangely, a scruffy-haired man performed an old Norse work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' reads as 'strangely' but means take the odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The sagas are prose narratives written in Iceland in the Middle Ages about heroes and families.

clue.text: Bird that's black and gold returning home

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: B is the pencil abbreviation for black
or is heraldic gold
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: A black and golden bird flies back to its nest.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold; the black-and-gold pair goes backwards before home is added.
explanation.definitionFit: The robin is a small songbird with a red breast.

clue.text: King and Queen whisked away from naked celebrities

indicators.note: whisking something away removes it, so letters are taken out

parts.note: starkers is British slang for stark naked
K for king, as in chess
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: Royals are hurried away from a crowd of famous people in the nude.
explanation.walkthrough: Starkers is British slang for naked; remove the king and queen abbreviations from inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Famous performers are called stars, as in the stars of the screen.

clue.text: One turned on by mild garlic?

parts.note: light means gentle or not strong
garlic grows as a bulb

explanation.surface: Someone who finds gentle garlic arousing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' suggests excitement, but it means switched on.
explanation.definitionFit: Electric lamps are switched on, so the glass globe that glows is something you turn on.

clue.text: Anticipation created by South American writer's penultimate part of novel

parts.note: the compass abbreviation
the United States
a pen writes, plus the possessive s

indicators.note: penultimate means last but one, so that letter alone is kept

parts.note: the fourth of five letters

explanation.surface: Tension built up by a Latin American author near the end of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American writer' wants to be one person; it splits into a compass point, a country and a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspense is the tense excitement of waiting to learn what happens.

clue.text: Lawmaker in unfamiliar borough taking week off

indicators.note: taking time off means being absent, so a letter goes missing

parts.note: new means not known before
a borough is a town

explanation.surface: A legislator in a strange town goes on a week's holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lawmaker' suggests a politician; it is the scientist behind the laws of motion. W is the abbreviation for week.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion and gravitation, so he made laws of physics.
